# Work With Kaggle

Use this skill whenever the task involves Kaggle notebooks, kernels, datasets, or GPU validation runs.

## Project Memory First

For project repositories, read local project guidance before changing notebooks or source:

- `AGENTS.md`
- `memory/PROMPTS.md` and `memory/CHANGELOG.md`, especially recent Kaggle entries
- relevant `test_results/kaggle_*` reports for the same failure/config family

This project has many Kaggle-specific decisions preserved in memory. Do not assume a generic Kaggle workflow is correct when project memory says otherwise.

## Safety And Scope

- Do not upload or publish current uncommitted source to a Kaggle dataset unless the user explicitly approves external export.
- Prefer GitHub-backed Kaggle source when the user has selected GitHub as source of truth.
- Do not push a public Kaggle notebook/kernel unless the user explicitly approves publication or public push.
- Do not make C++/CUDA algorithmic changes while diagnosing Kaggle failures unless the user explicitly approves code changes. Config-only notebook changes are acceptable when useful and consistent with the request.
- Do not revert unrelated local changes. Kaggle notebook edits often coexist with dirty source changes.
- For multi-rank validation, do not fake `WORLD_SIZE=2` on one <truncated omitted_approx_tokens="707" />ed logs. This rule came from project memory and applies to diagnostic/watch tasks.
- Do not stop production/no-timeout runs unless the user explicitly asks or the notebook itself has a configured timeout.
- If a run appears hung because stdout is redirected, check rank log files and whether live-rank streaming is enabled before assuming a stall.
- Preserve logs even when stopping: terminate gracefully when possible, then download output files.

## Failure Diagnosis Checklist

After a Kaggle failure, collect and scan:

- Kaggle worker status and kernel version
- notebook stdout tail
- rank logs under the notebook output directory
- result JSONL/CSV summaries
- GPU budget/preflight output
- explicit Kaggle messages such as disk quota failures

Common patterns in this project:

- `KernelWorkerStatus.ERROR` plus "more disk space than is available" usually means disk quota/static history arena pressure.
- `return_code=-9` can indicate host RAM OOM.
- `code=3002` / `STREAM_FATAL_STREAM3_DOUBLE_BUFFER_OVERFLOW` points to Stream3/Stream4/threshold/capacity flow diagnostics.
- `final selected count does not match score phase counts` points to final selection/histogram/exact-count mismatch.
- `cudaGraphInstantiate: out of memory` may require config-only headroom/shard-capacity changes before deeper code work.
- Silent output after build may simply mean rank stdout is redirected and live rank logging is disabled.

Write a short report under `test_results/` for meaningful Kaggle validations, sweeps, failures, or launches.

## Response Style

- Be explicit about whether you changed source code, notebook config only, or only launched/monitored a run.
- Include Kaggle kernel slug/version/status when known.
- Include exact local report/log paths in `test_results/`.
- Keep recommendations tied to evidence from logs, not guesses.
- If the next step requires exporting source or publishing publicly, ask for explicit approval first.

# Work With Kaggle

Use this skill whenever the task involves Kaggle notebooks, kernels, datasets, or GPU validation runs.

## Project Memory First

For project repositories, read local project guidance before changing notebooks or source:

- `AGENTS.md`
- `memory/PROMPTS.md` and `memory/CHANGELOG.md`, especially recent Kaggle entries
- relevant `test_results/kaggle_*` reports for the same failure/config family

This project has many Kaggle-specific decisions preserved in memory. Do not assume a generic Kaggle workflow is correct when project memory says otherwise.

## Safety And Scope

- Do not upload or publish current uncommitted source to a Kaggle dataset unless the user explicitly approves external export.
- Prefer GitHub-backed Kaggle source when the user has selected GitHub as source of truth.
- Do not push a public Kaggle notebook/kernel unless the user explicitly approves publication or public push.
- Do not make C++/CUDA algorithmic changes while diagnosing Kaggle failures unless the user explicitly approves code changes. Config-only notebook changes are acceptable when useful and consistent with the request.
- Do not revert unrelated local changes. Kaggle notebook edits often coexist with dirty source changes.
- For multi-rank validation, do not fake `WORLD_SIZE=2` on one <truncated omitted_approx_tokens="707" />ed logs. This rule came from project memory and applies to diagnostic/watch tasks.
- Do not stop production/no-timeout runs unless the user explicitly asks or the notebook itself has a configured timeout.
- If a run appears hung because stdout is redirected, check rank log files and whether live-rank streaming is enabled before assuming a stall.
- Preserve logs even when stopping: terminate gracefully when possible, then download output files.

## Failure Diagnosis Checklist

After a Kaggle failure, collect and scan:

- Kaggle worker status and kernel version
- notebook stdout tail
- rank logs under the notebook output directory
- result JSONL/CSV summaries
- GPU budget/preflight output
- explicit Kaggle messages such as disk quota failures

Common patterns in this project:

- `KernelWorkerStatus.ERROR` plus "more disk space than is available" usually means disk quota/static history arena pressure.
- `return_code=-9` can indicate host RAM OOM.
- `code=3002` / `STREAM_FATAL_STREAM3_DOUBLE_BUFFER_OVERFLOW` points to Stream3/Stream4/threshold/capacity flow diagnostics.
- `final selected count does not match score phase counts` points to final selection/histogram/exact-count mismatch.
- `cudaGraphInstantiate: out of memory` may require config-only headroom/shard-capacity changes before deeper code work.
- Silent output after build may simply mean rank stdout is redirected and live rank logging is disabled.

Write a short report under `test_results/` for meaningful Kaggle validations, sweeps, failures, or launches.

## Response Style

- Be explicit about whether you changed source code, notebook config only, or only launched/monitored a run.
- Include Kaggle kernel slug/version/status when known.
- Include exact local report/log paths in `test_results/`.
- Keep recommendations tied to evidence from logs, not guesses.
- If the next step requires exporting source or publishing publicly, ask for explicit approval first.

# Work With Kaggle

Use this skill whenever the task involves Kaggle notebooks, kernels, datasets, or GPU validation runs.

## Project Memory First

For project repositories, read local project guidance before changing notebooks or source:

- `AGENTS.md`
- `memory/PROMPTS.md` and `memory/CHANGELOG.md`, especially recent Kaggle entries
- relevant `test_results/kaggle_*` reports for the same failure/config family

This project has many Kaggle-specific decisions preserved in memory. Do not assume a generic Kaggle workflow is correct when project memory says otherwise.

## Safety And Scope

- Do not upload or publish current uncommitted source to a Kaggle dataset unless the user explicitly approves external export.
- Prefer GitHub-backed Kaggle source when the user has selected GitHub as source of truth.
- Do not push a public Kaggle notebook/kernel unless the user explicitly approves publication or public push.
- Do not make C++/CUDA algorithmic changes while diagnosing Kaggle failures unless the user explicitly approves code changes. Config-only notebook changes are acceptable when useful and consistent with the request.
- Do not revert unrelated local changes. Kaggle notebook edits often coexist with dirty source changes.
- For multi-rank validation, do not fake `WORLD_SIZE=2` on one <truncated omitted_approx_tokens="707" />ed logs. This rule came from project memory and applies to diagnostic/watch tasks.
- Do not stop production/no-timeout runs unless the user explicitly asks or the notebook itself has a configured timeout.
- If a run appears hung because stdout is redirected, check rank log files and whether live-rank streaming is enabled before assuming a stall.
- Preserve logs even when stopping: terminate gracefully when possible, then download output files.

## Failure Diagnosis Checklist

After a Kaggle failure, collect and scan:

- Kaggle worker status and kernel version
- notebook stdout tail
- rank logs under the notebook output directory
- result JSONL/CSV summaries
- GPU budget/preflight output
- explicit Kaggle messages such as disk quota failures

Common patterns in this project:

- `KernelWorkerStatus.ERROR` plus "more disk space than is available" usually means disk quota/static history arena pressure.
- `return_code=-9` can indicate host RAM OOM.
- `code=3002` / `STREAM_FATAL_STREAM3_DOUBLE_BUFFER_OVERFLOW` points to Stream3/Stream4/threshold/capacity flow diagnostics.
- `final selected count does not match score phase counts` points to final selection/histogram/exact-count mismatch.
- `cudaGraphInstantiate: out of memory` may require config-only headroom/shard-capacity changes before deeper code work.
- Silent output after build may simply mean rank stdout is redirected and live rank logging is disabled.

Write a short report under `test_results/` for meaningful Kaggle validations, sweeps, failures, or launches.

## Response Style

- Be explicit about whether you changed source code, notebook config only, or only launched/monitored a run.
- Include Kaggle kernel slug/version/status when known.
- Include exact local report/log paths in `test_results/`.
- Keep recommendations tied to evidence from logs, not guesses.
- If the next step requires exporting source or publishing publicly, ask for explicit approval first.

# Project Agent Rules

## Operating Rule
- Read `AGENTS.md` before project edits.
- Update `memory/CHANGELOG.md` after meaningful code, config, or architecture changes.
- Update `memory/PROMPTS.md` with user prompts that define requirements.
- Store test outputs, logs, and verification notes under `test_results/`.
- Prefer agent-centered code: explicit contracts, deterministic tests, small files, low hidden state.

## Architecture Source
- Primary architecture contract: `ARCHITECTURE_NEED.md`.
- Current Stream 4 implementation rule: use threshold + compact + CUB/fixed-temp sort/reduce + compact; do not use Stream 4 hash-table dedup.

## Implementation Guardrails
- `State128` logical bytes are `v[0..119]`.
- `State128` padding bytes are `v[120..127]`.
- Persistent frontier padding must be zero.
- `FinalResponse` may temporarily store `target_local_idx` in `v[120..123]`.
- `Hash128` is one logical 128-bit key stored as `{lo, hi}`.
- `CandidateMeta` must remain 32 bytes and 32-byte aligned.
- Stream 3 payload id must be original candidate id, not compact index.
- Stream 4 must not apply shard top-k or semantic shard cap.

# Changelog

## 2026-07-03

## 2026-07-01
- Ran Kaggle 2xT4 Stream1 piece-transformer benchmark version 4 after pushing commit `08d1ddd`. # Work With Kaggle

Use this skill whenever the task involves Kaggle notebooks, kernels, datasets, or GPU validation runs.

## Project Memory First

For project repositories, read local project guidance before changing notebooks or source:

- `AGENTS.md`
- `memory/PROMPTS.md` and `memory/CHANGELOG.md`, especially recent Kaggle entries
- relevant `test_results/kaggle_*` reports for the same failure/config family

This project has many Kaggle-specific decisions preserved in memory. Do not assume a generic Kaggle workflow is correct when project memory says otherwise.

## Safety And Scope

- Do not upload or publish current uncommitted source to a Kaggle dataset unless the user explicitly approves external export.
- Prefer GitHub-backed Kaggle source when the user has selected GitHub as source of truth.
- Do not push a public Kaggle notebook/kernel unless the user explicitly approves publication or public push.
- Do not make C++/CUDA algorithmic changes while diagnosing Kaggle failures unless the user explicitly approves code changes. Config-only notebook changes are acceptable when useful and consistent with the request.
- Do not revert unrelated local changes. Kaggle notebook edits often coexist with dirty source changes.
- For multi-rank validation, do not fake `WORLD_SIZE=2` on one <truncated omitted_approx_tokens="707" />ed logs. This rule came from project memory and applies to diagnostic/watch tasks.
- Do not stop production/no-timeout runs unless the user explicitly asks or the notebook itself has a configured timeout.
- If a run appears hung because stdout is redirected, check rank log files and whether live-rank streaming is enabled before assuming a stall.
- Preserve logs even when stopping: terminate gracefully when possible, then download output files.

## Failure Diagnosis Checklist

After a Kaggle failure, collect and scan:

- Kaggle worker status and kernel version
- notebook stdout tail
- rank logs under the notebook output directory
- result JSONL/CSV summaries
- GPU budget/preflight output
- explicit Kaggle messages such as disk quota failures

Common patterns in this project:

- `KernelWorkerStatus.ERROR` plus "more disk space than is available" usually means disk quota/static history arena pressure.
- `return_code=-9` can indicate host RAM OOM.
- `code=3002` / `STREAM_FATAL_STREAM3_DOUBLE_BUFFER_OVERFLOW` points to Stream3/Stream4/threshold/capacity flow diagnostics.
- `final selected count does not match score phase counts` points to final selection/histogram/exact-count mismatch.
- `cudaGraphInstantiate: out of memory` may require config-only headroom/shard-capacity changes before deeper code work.
- Silent output after build may simply mean rank stdout is redirected and live rank logging is disabled.

Write a short report under `test_results/` for meaningful Kaggle validations, sweeps, failures, or launches.

## Response Style

- Be explicit about whether you changed source code, notebook config only, or only launched/monitored a run.
- Include Kaggle kernel slug/version/status when known.
- Include exact local report/log paths in `test_results/`.
- Keep recommendations tied to evidence from logs, not guesses.
- If the next step requires exporting source or publishing publicly, ask for explicit approval first.

# Project Agent Rules

## Operating Rule
- Read `AGENTS.md` before project edits.
- Update `memory/CHANGELOG.md` after meaningful code, config, or architecture changes.
- Update `memory/PROMPTS.md` with user prompts that define requirements.
- Store test outputs, logs, and verification notes under `test_results/`.
- Prefer agent-centered code: explicit contracts, deterministic tests, small files, low hidden state.

## Architecture Source
- Primary architecture contract: `ARCHITECTURE_NEED.md`.
- Current Stream 4 implementation rule: use threshold + compact + CUB/fixed-temp sort/reduce + compact; do not use Stream 4 hash-table dedup.

## Implementation Guardrails
- `State128` logical bytes are `v[0..119]`.
- `State128` padding bytes are `v[120..127]`.
- Persistent frontier padding must be zero.
- `FinalResponse` may temporarily store `target_local_idx` in `v[120..123]`.
- `Hash128` is one logical 128-bit key stored as `{lo, hi}`.
- `CandidateMeta` must remain 32 bytes and 32-byte aligned.
- Stream 3 payload id must be original candidate id, not compact index.
- Stream 4 must not apply shard top-k or semantic shard cap.

# Changelog

## 2026-07-03
- Added a transformer-only Stream1 piece-transformer FF1 fused CUTLASS path: the first feed-forward GEMM now uses `GemmUniversalWithBroadcast` with bias+SiLU in the epilogue, removing the separate FF1 bias/SiLU CUDA kernel while leaving the MLP path and residual GEMMs unchanged. Docker verification passed `stream1_transformer_cuda_tests`, `contract_tests`, and `dispatcher_cuda_tests`; local SM86 smoke with `B_MICRO=512`, `concurrency=1` measured `582529.0` candidates/s. Evidence is recorded in `test_results/stream1_transformer_ff1_fused_2026-07-03.md`.
## 2026-07-01
- Ran Kaggle 2xT4 Stream1 piece-transformer benchmark version 4 after pushing commit `08d1ddd`. Fresh CUDA tensor-GEMM attention backend completed with best per-T4 rows: GPU0 `401869.4` candidates/s at `B_MICRO=1024, concurrency=1`; GPU1 `411356.9` candidates/s at `B_MICRO=512, concurrency=2`; aggregate `813226.3` candidates/s. This is `~0.55x` of direct PyTorch fast forward and `~0.64-0.65x` of PyTorch `batch_process`, so it is not a hard ceiling. Evidence is recorded in `test_results/transformer_inference_example_kaggle_speed_2026-07-01.md`.

## Scope

- Kernel: `trydotatwo/cayley-beam-transformer-2xt4-benchmark`

This run only validates the graph-replay benchmark path on Kaggle 2xT4. No CUDA source or MLP-path behavior was changed for this launch.

## Local Preflight

- `kernel-metadata.json` inspected: private notebook, `NvidiaTeslaT4`, model source `vladkuznetsov266/megaminx-qtransformer-1782210824/PyTorch/default/1`.

  - per-GPU benchmark env includes `BEAM_STREAM1_TRANSFORMER_GRAPH_BENCH=1`

## Output Location

- `test_results/kaggle_stream1_transformer_2xt4_v10_graph_2026-07-03/`

- CSV: `test_results/kaggle_stream1_transformer_2xt4_v10_graph_2026-07-03/stream1_transformer_benchmark_rows.csv`

CUDA graph replay on Kaggle T4 does not materially improve the isolated Stream1 transformer benchmark.  # Changelog
 
 ## 2026-07-03
+- Ran Kaggle 2xT4 benchmark version 10 against tag `stream1-transformer-graph-bench-e35432d` with `BEAM_STREAM1_TRANSFORMER_GRAPH_BENCH=1`. The run completed successfully: best T4 throughput was `468639.3` candidates/s on GPU0 and `462338.7` on GPU1, aggregate `930978.0` candidates/s. This is about `0.989x` of the previous v9 QKV-fused benchmark, so graph replay alone does not close the PyTorch gap. Evidence: `test_results/stream1_transformer_kaggle_benchmark_v10_graph_2026-07-03.md`.
 - Added a transformer-only Stream1 piece-transformer FF1 fused CUTLASS path: the first feed-forward GEMM now uses `GemmUniversalWithBroadcast` with bias+SiLU in the epilogue, removing the separate FF1 bias/SiLU CUDA kernel while leaving the MLP path and residual GEMMs unchanged. Docker verification passed `stream1_transformer_cuda_tests`, `contract_tests`, and `dispatcher_cuda_tests`; local SM86 smoke with `B_MICRO=512`, `concurrency=1` measured `582529.0` candidates/s. Evidence is recorded in `test_results/stream1_transformer_ff1_fused_2026-07-03.md`.
 ## 2026-07-01
 - Ran Kaggle 2xT4 Stream1 piece-transformer benchmark version 4 after pushing commit `08d1ddd`. Fresh CUDA tensor-GEMM attention backend completed with best per-T4 rows: GPU0 `401869.4` candidates/s at `B_MICRO=1024, concurrency=1`; GPU1 `411356.9` candidates/s at `B_MICRO=512, concurrency=2`; aggregate `813226.3` candidates/s. This is `~0.55x` of direct PyTorch fast forward and `~0.64-0.65x` of PyTorch `batch_process`, so it is not a hard ceiling. Evidence is recorded in `test_results/stream1_transformer_kaggle_benchmark_v4_2026-07-01.md`.

## Scope

- Kernel: `trydotatwo/cayley-beam-transformer-2xt4-benchmark`

This run only validates the graph-replay benchmark path on Kaggle 2xT4. No CUDA source or MLP-path behavior was changed for this launch.

## Local Preflight

- `kernel-metadata.json` inspected: private notebook, `NvidiaTeslaT4`, model source `vladkuznetsov266/megaminx-qtransformer-1782210824/PyTorch/default/1`.
- Notebook JSON parse: pass.

  - `GITHUB_EXPECTED_COMMIT = "e35432d"`
  - per-GPU benchmark env includes `BEAM_STREAM1_TRANSFORMER_GRAPH_BENCH=1`

## Output Location

Downloaded Kaggle artifacts:

- `test_results/kaggle_stream1_transformer_2xt4_v10_graph_2026-07-03/`

- CSV: `test_results/kaggle_stream1_transformer_2xt4_v10_graph_2026-07-03/stream1_transformer_benchmark_rows.csv`

## Results

Best lines from the Kaggle log:

- GPU0: `b_micro=1024`, `concurrency=1`, `candidates_per_sec=468639.3`, `scratch_bytes=327729152`
- GPU1: `b_micro=512`, `concurrency=2`, `candidates_per_sec=462338.7`, `scratch_bytes=327729152`
- Aggregate: `STREAM1_TRANSFORMER_BEST_2XT4_AGG_CANDIDATES_PER_SEC=930978.0`

The per-report files both show `graph_bench=1` and `status=pass`.

## Comparison

Previous Kaggle v9 QKV-fused benchmark:

- GPU0: `474114.7` candidates/s
- GPU1: `467352.5` candidates/s
- Aggregate: `941467.2` candidates/s

Graph replay v10 is therefore about:

- GPU0: `0.988x` of v9
- GPU1: `0.989x` of v9
- Aggregate: `0.989x` of v9

PyTorch reference from the transformer inference example was about `630697.0` candidates/s per T4 in the searcher-like `batch_process` mode, so v10 native graph replay reaches about `0.74x` / `0.73x` of that reference.

## Interpretation

CUDA graph replay on Kaggle T4 does not materially improve the isolated Stream1 transformer benchmark. This matches the local Nsight finding: launch overhead is no longer the main bottleneck under graph replay. The remaining gap is still in transformer linear GEMMs, LayerNorm/copy work, attention layout, and remaining unfused epilogues.

**Главное отличие**
PyTorch в блоке делает attention как один высокоуровневый `F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q,k,v)` и backend сам выбирает fused SDPA kernel. См. [model.py](D:/100XH100/.worktrees/stream1-piece-transformer/test_results/kaggle_model_artifact_download/megaminx-transformer/pilgrim/model.py:218).

Наш T4 path attention разложен вручную:
- 8 запусков QK `GemmBatched`, по одному на head
- отдельный `pack_v51`
- отдельный `softmax51`
- 8 запусков PV `GemmBatched`
- это повторяется на каждый transformer layer

Код: [cuda/stream1_transformer.cu](D:/100XH100/.worktrees/stream1-piece-transformer/cuda/stream1_transformer.cu:841).

**Что уже сравняли**
- QKV теперь уже `GEMM + bias` в CUTLASS epilogue, не отдельный bias kernel.
- FF1 теперь уже `GEMM + bias + SiLU`.
- Graph replay проверили: почти не помог, значит проблема не в host launch overhead.

**Что еще хуже PyTorch**
1. Attention layout: PyTorch не гоняет полный `scores -> softmax -> probs -> V pack` через наши отдельные scratch-проходы. Наш код пишет/читает `attention_scores_probs` и `attention_context` глобально.
2. LayerNorm: у нас отдельный кастомный `layernorm256_copy_kernel`, в Nsight это было ~15% GPU time. PyTorch использует хорошо оптимизированный LN.
3. Residual+bias: у нас `attn_out` и `ff2` делают residual GEMM, потом отдельный `bias_add_kernel`. PyTorch выражает это как `x + matmul + bias`, и backend/Inductor/cuBLASLt лучше склеивает такие хвосты.
4. Linear kernels: PyTorch/cuBLASLt авто-подбирает kernel под shape. У нас CUTLASS tiles фиксированы, и для мелких transformer GEMM это не всегда лучший выбор.

**По цифрам**
- PyTorch fast `batch_process`: `630697 candidates/s` на T4.
- Наш v10 graph replay: `468639` и `462339 candidates/s`.
- То есть мы примерно `0.73-0.74x` от PyTorch, не катастрофа, но gap реальный.

Вывод: следующий реальный фикс не graph и не batch tuning, а T4 fused short-SDPA backend: один attention path для `seq=51, heads=8, head_dim=32`, без полного materialize `scores/probs` и без 16 head-GEMM launches на слой. Потом уже добивать LayerNorm и residual+bias epilogues.

# HighloadGpu

Router for CUDA code-writing and high-performance GPU engineering. Default to a single-GPU CUDA hot path first; use multi-GPU or search/decoding guidance only when the task calls for it.

## Pick The Sub-Skill

- CUDA kernels, memory layout, CUTLASS/CUB, graphs, native hot paths: `write-cuda-hot-paths`
- Beam search, top-k/top-p decoding, frontier expansion, candidate selection: `optimize-gpu-search-and-decoding`
- Multi-GPU scaling, rank ownership, peer access, NCCL, overlap: `design-multigpu-systems`
- Python/Rust/C++/CUDA ownership boundaries: `choose-stack-boundaries`
- GPU model, compute capability, CUDA/library docs: `use-nvidia-docs`
- Timeline/stream/NCCL/launch gaps: `use-nsight-systems`
- One-kernel bottleneck: `use-nsight-compute`
- Illegal access/race/init/sync bug: `use-compute-sanitizer`
- Batch/concurrency/shard sweeps: `benchmark-and-sweep-gpu-configs`
- Kaggle/Molab/remote GPU profiling: `profile-remote-gpu-runs`

## Defaults

- Python: wrappers, notebooks, dashboards, CLI/torchrun launch.
- Rust: safe config, validation, artifact/log tooling, host services.
- C++ + CUDA: CPU/GPU hot paths, kernels, CUDA Graphs, NCCL, CUTLASS, CUB/CCCL.

Check current NVIDIA docs before hardware-specific advice. Require correctness checks and profiling evidence before architecture changes.

name: write-cuda-hot-paths
description: Use when writing or optimizing CUDA kernels, memory layouts, and GPU hot paths.
---

# Write CUDA Hot Paths

Primary skill for CUDA code-writing. Hot paths are fixed-capacity, allocation-free, profiler-driven, and explicit about layout, alignment, ownership, and synchronization.

## Workflow

1. State shapes, precision, target GPU,<truncated omitted_approx_tokens="76" />s.
- Use explicit capacity guards; fail loudly on overflow.
- Keep CPU readback out of the steady-state path.
- Use CUDA Graphs for repeated launch templates; keep dynamic dispatch on host.
- Add static asserts for cross-kernel metadata size/alignment.
- Store only downstream-needed data; avoid materializing large intermediates when compact keys, indices, or reductions are enough.

## Library Defaults

CUTLASS/cuBLAS for GEMM/tensor-core kernels; CUB/CCCL for sort/reduce/scan/select; NCCL for GPU exchange/collectives; CUDA Runtime/Driver APIs for memory, streams, events, graphs, devices, and peer access.

## Avoid

Dynamic `cudaMalloc`, Python data-plane loops, fine-grained atomics when partition/sort/scan works, custom sort before checking CUB/CCCL, and synchronization that hides ownership bugs.
# Project Agent Rules

## Operating Rule
- Read `AGENTS.md` before project edits.
- Update `memory/CHANGELOG.md` after meaningful code, config, or architecture changes.
- Update `memory/PROMPTS.md` with user prompts that define requirements.
- Store test outputs, logs, and verification notes under `test_results/`.
- Prefer agent-centered code: explicit contracts, deterministic tests, small files, low hidden state.

## Architecture Source
- Primary architecture contract: `ARCHITECTURE_NEED.md`.
- Current Stream 4 implementation rule: use threshold + compact + CUB/fixed-temp sort/reduce + compact; do not use Stream 4 hash-table dedup.

## Implementation Guardrails
- `State128` logical bytes are `v[0..119]`.
- `State128` padding bytes are `v[120..127]`.
- Persistent frontier padding must be zero.
- `FinalResponse` may temporarily store `target_local_idx` in `v[120..123]`.
- `Hash128` is one logical 128-bit key stored as `{lo, hi}`.
- `CandidateMeta` must remain 32 bytes and 32-byte aligned.
- Stream 3 payload id must be original candidate id, not compact index.
- Stream 4 must not apply shard top-k or semantic shard cap.

[1108] assistant: Разница не в модели. Модельная математика та же: fast piece-cache, 4 pre-norm блока, QKV, SDPA, FFN, output. Разница в том, как это исполняется.

**Главное отличие**
PyTorch в блоке делает attention как один высокоуровневый `F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q,k,v)` и backend сам выбирает fused SDPA kernel. См. [model.py](D:/100XH100/.worktrees/stream1-piece-transformer/test_results/kaggle_model_artifact_download/megaminx-transformer/pilgrim/model.py:218).

Наш T4 path attention разложен вручную:
- 8 запусков QK `GemmBatched`, по одному на head
- отдельный `pack_v51`
- отдельный `softmax51`
- 8 запусков PV `GemmBatched`
- это повторяется на каждый transformer layer

Код: [cuda/stream1_transformer.cu](D:/100XH100/.worktrees/stream1-piece-transformer/cuda/stream1_transformer.cu:841).

**Что уже сравняли**
- QKV теперь уже `GEMM + bias` в CUTLASS epilogue, не отдельный bias kernel.
- FF1 теперь уже `GEMM + bias + SiLU`.
- Graph replay проверили: почти не помог, значит проблема не в host launch overhead.

**Что еще хуже PyTorch**
1. Attention layout: PyTorch не гоняет полный `scores -> softmax -> probs -> V pack` через наши отдельные scratch-проходы. Наш код пишет/читает `attention_scores_probs` и `attention_context` глобально.
2. LayerNorm: у нас отдельный кастомный `layernorm256_copy_kernel`, в Nsight это было ~15% GPU time. PyTorch использует хорошо оптимизированный LN.
3. Residual+bias: у нас `attn_out` и `ff2` делают residual GEMM, потом отдельный `bias_add_kernel`. PyTorch выражает это как `x + matmul + bias`, и backend/Inductor/cuBLASLt лучше склеивает такие хвосты.
4. Linear kernels: PyTorch/cuBLASLt авто-подбирает kernel под shape. У нас CUTLASS tiles фиксированы, и для мелких transformer GEMM это не всегда лучший выбор.

**По цифрам**
- PyTorch fast `batch_process`: `630697 candidates/s` на T4.
- Наш v10 graph replay: `468639` и `462339 candidates/s`.
- То есть мы примерно `0.73-0.74x` от PyTorch, не катастрофа, но gap реальный.

Вывод: следующий реальный фикс не graph и не batch tuning, а T4 fused short-SDPA backend: один attention path для `seq=51, heads=8, head_dim=32`, без полного materialize `scores/probs` и без 16 head-GEMM launches на слой. Потом уже добивать LayerNorm и residual+bias epilogues.

# HighloadGpu

Router for CUDA code-writing and high-performance GPU engineering. Default to a single-GPU CUDA hot path first; use multi-GPU or search/decoding guidance only when the task calls for it.

## Pick The Sub-Skill

- CUDA kernels, memory layout, CUTLASS/CUB, graphs, native hot paths: `write-cuda-hot-paths`
- Beam search, top-k/top-p decoding, frontier expansion, candidate selection: `optimize-gpu-search-and-decoding`
- Multi-GPU scaling, rank ownership, peer access, NCCL, overlap: `design-multigpu-systems`
- Python/Rust/C++/CUDA ownership boundaries: `choose-stack-boundaries`
- GPU model, compute capability, CUDA/library docs: `use-nvidia-docs`
- Timeline/stream/NCCL/launch gaps: `use-nsight-systems`
- One-kernel bottleneck: `use-nsight-compute`
- Illegal access/race/init/sync bug: `use-compute-sanitizer`
- Batch/concurrency/shard sweeps: `benchmark-and-sweep-gpu-configs`
- Kaggle/Molab/remote GPU profiling: `profile-remote-gpu-runs`

## Defaults

- Python: wrappers, notebooks, dashboards, CLI/torchrun launch.
- Rust: safe config, validation, artifact/log tooling, host services.
- C++ + CUDA: CPU/GPU hot paths, kernels, CUDA Graphs, NCCL, CUTLASS, CUB/CCCL.

Check current NVIDIA docs before hardware-specific advice. Require correctness checks and profiling evidence before architecture changes.

name: write-cuda-hot-paths
description: Use when writing or optimizing CUDA kernels, memory layouts, and GPU hot paths.

# Write CUDA Hot Paths

Primary skill for CUDA code-writing. Hot paths are fixed-capacity, allocation-free, profiler-driven, and explicit about layout, alignment, ownership, and synchronization.

## Workflow

1. State shapes, precision, target GPU,<truncated omitted_approx_tokens="76" />s.
- Use explicit capacity guards; fail loudly on overflow.
- Keep CPU readback out of the steady-state path.
- Use CUDA Graphs for repeated launch templates; keep dynamic dispatch on host.
- Add static asserts for cross-kernel metadata size/alignment.
- Store only downstream-needed data; avoid materializing large intermediates when compact keys, indices, or reductions are enough.

## Library Defaults

CUTLASS/cuBLAS for GEMM/tensor-core kernels; CUB/CCCL for sort/reduce/scan/select; NCCL for GPU exchange/collectives; CUDA Runtime/Driver APIs for memory, streams, events, graphs, devices, and peer access.

## Avoid

Dynamic `cudaMalloc`, Python data-plane loops, fine-grained atomics when partition/sort/scan works, custom sort before checking CUB/CCCL, and synchronization that hides ownership bugs.
# Project Agent Rules

## Operating Rule
- Read `AGENTS.md` before project edits.
- Update `memory/CHANGELOG.md` after meaningful code, config, or architecture changes.
- Update `memory/PROMPTS.md` with user prompts that define requirements.
- Store test outputs, logs, and verification notes under `test_results/`.
- Prefer agent-centered code: explicit contracts, deterministic tests, small files, low hidden state.

## Architecture Source
- Primary architecture contract: `ARCHITECTURE_NEED.md`.
- Current Stream 4 implementation rule: use threshold + compact + CUB/fixed-temp sort/reduce + compact; do not use Stream 4 hash-table dedup.

## Implementation Guardrails
- `State128` logical bytes are `v[0..119]`.
- `State128` padding bytes are `v[120..127]`.
- Persistent frontier padding must be zero.
- `FinalResponse` may temporarily store `target_local_idx` in `v[120..123]`.
- `Hash128` is one logical 128-bit key stored as `{lo, hi}`.
- `CandidateMeta` must remain 32 bytes and 32-byte aligned.
- Stream 3 payload id must be original candidate id, not compact index.
- Stream 4 must not apply shard top-k or semantic shard cap.

constexpr std::uint32_t FMHA_SEQ51 = 51U;
constexpr std::uint32_t FMHA_DMODEL256 = 256U;
constexpr std::uint32_t FMHA_HEAD_DIM32 = 32U;
constexpr std::uint32_t FMHA_NHEAD8 = 8U;
constexpr std::uint32_t FMHA_QKV_STRIDE51 = 3U * FMHA_DMODEL256;

__device__ float stream1_fmha_load_scalar_device(const half* ptr, std::uint64_t idx, std::uint32_t dtype) {
    if (dtype == STREAM1_DTYPE_BF16) {
        return __bfloat162float(reinterpret_cast<const __nv_bfloat16*>(ptr)[idx]);
    }
    return __half2float(ptr[idx]);
}

__device__ void stream1_fmha_store_scalar_device(half* ptr, std::uint64_t idx, float value, std::uint32_t dtype) {
    if (dtype == STREAM1_DTYPE_BF16) {
        reinterpret_cast<__nv_bfloat16*>(ptr)[idx] = __float2bfloat16(value);
        return;
    }
    ptr[idx] = __float2half(value);
}

 # Changelog
 
 ## 2026-07-03
+- Routed Stream1 `piece_transformer` attention through CUTLASS FMHA for the PyTorch-like SDPA step: fp16 on SM75/T4 now uses `AttentionKernel<half, Sm75>`, fp16 on SM80+ uses `AttentionKernel<half, Sm80>`, and bf16 on SM80+ keeps `AttentionKernel<bfloat16, Sm80>`. The legacy decomposed tensor-attention backend was removed from dispatch, so missing FMHA support fails closed instead of falling back. MLP Stream1 files were not touched. Docker verification rebuilt SM75/SM86 targets and passed `stream1_transformer_cuda_tests`, `dispatcher_cuda_tests`, and `contract_tests`; local SM86 graph point `B_MICRO=1024`, `concurrency=4` measured `613097.9` candidates/s under a noisy concurrent GPU load. Evidence: `test_results/stream1_transformer_fmha_sdpa_route_2026-07-03.md`.
 - Ran Kaggle 2xT4 benchmark version 10 against tag `stream1-transformer-graph-bench-e35432d` with `BEAM_STREAM1_TRANSFORMER_GRAPH_BENCH=1`. The run completed successfully: best T4 throughput was `468639.3` candidates/s on GPU0 and `462338.7` on GPU1, aggregate `930978.0` candidates/s. This is about `0.989x` of the previous v9 QKV-fused benchmark, so graph replay alone does not close the PyTorch gap. Evidence: `test_results/stream1_transformer_kaggle_benchmark_v10_graph_2026-07-03.md`.
 - Added a transformer-only Stream1 piece-transformer FF1 fused CUTLASS path: the first feed-forward GEMM now uses `GemmUniversalWithBroadcast` with bias+SiLU in the epilogue, removing the separate FF1 bias/SiLU CUDA kernel while leaving the MLP path and residual GEMMs unchanged. Docker verification passed `stream1_transformer_cuda_tests`, `contract_tests`, and `dispatcher_cuda_tests`; local SM86 smoke with `B_MICRO=512`, `concurrency=1` measured `582529.0` candidates/s. Evidence is recorded in `test_results/stream1_transformer_ff1_fused_2026-07-03.md`.

 # Changelog
 
 ## 2026-07-03
+- Routed Stream1 `piece_transformer` attention through CUTLASS FMHA for the PyTorch-like SDPA step: fp16 on SM75/T4 now uses `AttentionKernel<half, Sm75>`, fp16 on SM80+ uses `AttentionKernel<half, Sm80>`, and bf16 on SM80+ keeps `AttentionKernel<bfloat16, Sm80>`. The legacy decomposed tensor-attention backend was removed from dispatch, so missing FMHA support fails closed instead of falling back. MLP Stream1 files were not touched. Docker verification rebuilt SM75/SM86 targets and passed `stream1_transformer_cuda_tests`, `dispatcher_cuda_tests`, and `contract_tests`; local SM86 graph point `B_MICRO=1024`, `concurrency=4` measured `613097.9` candidates/s under a noisy concurrent GPU load. Evidence: `test_results/stream1_transformer_fmha_sdpa_route_2026-07-03.md`.
 - Ran Kaggle 2xT4 benchmark version 10 against tag `stream1-transformer-graph-bench-e35432d` with `BEAM_STREAM1_TRANSFORMER_GRAPH_BENCH=1`. The run completed successfully: best T4 throughput was `468639.3` candidates/s on GPU0 and `462338.7` on GPU1, aggregate `930978.0` candidates/s. This is about `0.989x` of the previous v9 QKV-fused benchmark, so graph replay alone does not close the PyTorch gap. Evidence: `test_results/stream1_transformer_kaggle_benchmark_v10_graph_2026-07-03.md`.
 - Added a transformer-only Stream1 piece-transformer FF1 fused CUTLASS path: the first feed-forward GEMM now uses `GemmUniversalWithBroadcast` with bias+SiLU in the epilogue, removing the separate FF1 bias/SiLU CUDA kernel while leaving the MLP path and residual GEMMs unchanged. Docker verification passed `stream1_transformer_cuda_tests`, `contract_tests`, and `dispatcher_cuda_tests`; local SM86 smoke with `B_MICRO=512`, `concurrency=1` measured `582529.0` candidates/s. Evidence is recorded in `test_results/stream1_transformer_ff1_fused_2026-07-03.md`.
 ## 2026-07-01

# Work With Kaggle

Use this skill whenever the task involves Kaggle notebooks, kernels, datasets, or GPU validation runs.

## Project Memory First

For project repositories, read local project guidance before changing notebooks or source:

- `AGENTS.md`
- `memory/PROMPTS.md` and `memory/CHANGELOG.md`, especially recent Kaggle entries
- relevant `test_results/kaggle_*` reports for the same failure/config family

This project has many Kaggle-specific decisions preserved in memory. Do not assume a generic Kaggle workflow is correct when project memory says otherwise.

## Safety And Scope

- Do not upload or publish current uncommitted source to a Kaggle dataset unless the user explicitly approves external export.
- Prefer GitHub-backed Kaggle source when the user has selected GitHub as source of truth.
- Do not push a public Kaggle notebook/kernel unless the user explicitly approves publication or public push.
- Do not make C++/CUDA algorithmic changes while diagnosing Kaggle failures unless the user explicitly approves code changes. Config-only notebook changes are acceptable when useful and consistent with the request.
- Do not revert unrelated local changes. Kaggle notebook edits often coexist with dirty source changes.
- For multi-rank validation, do not fake `WORLD_SIZE=2` on one <truncated omitted_approx_tokens="707" />ed logs. This rule came from project memory and applies to diagnostic/watch tasks.
- Do not stop production/no-timeout runs unless the user explicitly asks or the notebook itself has a configured timeout.
- If a run appears hung because stdout is redirected, check rank log files and whether live-rank streaming is enabled before assuming a stall.
- Preserve logs even when stopping: terminate gracefully when possible, then download output files.

## Failure Diagnosis Checklist

After a Kaggle failure, collect and scan:

- Kaggle worker status and kernel version
- notebook stdout tail
- rank logs under the notebook output directory
- result JSONL/CSV summaries
- GPU budget/preflight output
- explicit Kaggle messages such as disk quota failures

Common patterns in this project:

- `KernelWorkerStatus.ERROR` plus "more disk space than is available" usually means disk quota/static history arena pressure.
- `return_code=-9` can indicate host RAM OOM.
- `code=3002` / `STREAM_FATAL_STREAM3_DOUBLE_BUFFER_OVERFLOW` points to Stream3/Stream4/threshold/capacity flow diagnostics.
- `final selected count does not match score phase counts` points to final selection/histogram/exact-count mismatch.
- `cudaGraphInstantiate: out of memory` may require config-only headroom/shard-capacity changes before deeper code work.
- Silent output after build may simply mean rank stdout is redirected and live rank logging is disabled.

Write a short report under `test_results/` for meaningful Kaggle validations, sweeps, failures, or launches.

## Response Style

- Be explicit about whether you changed source code, notebook config only, or only launched/monitored a run.
- Include Kaggle kernel slug/version/status when known.
- Include exact local report/log paths in `test_results/`.
- Keep recommendations tied to evidence from logs, not guesses.
- If the next step requires exporting source or publishing publicly, ask for explicit approval first.

# Changelog

## 2026-07-03
- Ran Kaggle 2xT4 benchmark version 11 against tag `stream1-transformer-fmha-44352f1`. The CUTLASS FMHA attention route completed successfully with best T4 throughput `502218.5` candidates/s on GPU0 and `500790.0` on GPU1, aggregate `1003008.5` candidates/s. This is `1.077x` of v10 graph replay and about `0.80x` of the PyTorch SDPA reference. Evidence: `test_results/stream1_transformer_kaggle_benchmark_v11_fmha_2026-07-03.md`.
- Improved the Stream1 `piece_transformer` FMHA route by removing the explicit QKV repack kernel and passing the original QKV projection buffer directly to CUTLASS FMHA via strided Q/K/V pointers. Docker verification rebuilt SM75/SM86 targets and passed `stream1_transformer_cuda_tests`, `dispatcher_cuda_tests`, and `contract_tests`; local SM86 graph points reached `698530.6` candidates/s at `512x2` and `737089.2` at `1024x1`. Evidence: 	est_results/stream1_transformer_fmha_strided_qkv_2026-07-03.md.
- Updated `kaggle_t4_transformer_benchmark/t4-transformer-stream1-benchmark.ipynb` to pin the next 2xT4 Stream1 transformer benchmark to tag `stream1-transformer-fmha-44352f1` with expected commit prefix `44352f1`. Notebook JSON and code-cell AST validation passed.
- Routed Stream1 `piece_transformer` attention through CUTLASS FMHA for the PyTorch-like SDPA step: fp16 on SM75/T4 now uses `AttentionKernel<half, Sm75>`, fp16 on SM80+ uses `AttentionKernel<half, Sm80>`, and bf16 on SM80+ keeps `AttentionKernel<bfloat16, Sm80>`. The legacy decomposed tensor-attention backend was removed from dispatch, so missing FMHA support fails closed instead of falling back. MLP Stream1 files were not touched. Docker verification rebuilt SM75/SM86 targets and passed `stream1_transformer_cuda_tests`, `dispatcher_cuda_tests`, and `contract_tests`; local SM86 graph point `B_MICRO=1024`, `concurrency=4` measured `<truncated omitted_approx_tokens="68" />T4 throughput was `468639.3` candidates/s on GPU0 and `462338.7` on GPU1, aggregate `930978.0` candidates/s. This is about `0.989x` of the previous v9 QKV-fused benchmark, so graph replay alone does not close the PyTorch gap. Evidence: `test_results/stream1_transformer_kaggle_benchmark_v10_graph_2026-07-03.md`.
- Added a transformer-only Stream1 piece-transformer FF1 fused CUTLASS path: the first feed-forward GEMM now uses `GemmUniversalWithBroadcast` with bias+SiLU in the epilogue, removing the separate FF1 bias/SiLU CUDA kernel while leaving the MLP path and residual GEMMs unchanged. Docker verification passed `stream1_transformer_cuda_tests`, `contract_tests`, and `dispatcher_cuda_tests`; local SM86 smoke with `B_MICRO=512`, `concurrency=1` measured `582529.0` candidates/s. Evidence is recorded in `test_results/stream1_transformer_ff1_fused_2026-07-03.md`.
## 2026-07-01
- Ran Kaggle 2xT4 Stream1 piece-transformer benchmark version 4 after pushing commit `08d1ddd`. Fresh CUDA tensor-GEMM attention backend completed with best per-T4 rows: GPU0 `401869.4` candidates/s at `B_MICRO=1024, concurrency=1`; GPU1 `411356.9` candidates/s at `B_MICRO=512, concurrency=2`; aggregate `813226.3` candidates/s. This is `~0.55x` of direct PyTorch fast forward and `~0.64-0.65x` of PyTorch `batch_process`, so it is not a hard ceiling. Evidence is recorded in `test_results/stream1_transformer_kaggle_benchmark_v4_2026-07-01.md`.
- Added `kaggle_transformer_inference_speed/`, a private Kaggle script-kernel derived from `vladkuznetsov266/transformer-inference-example` to benchmark the model artifact inference speed directly. Version 2 completed on Tesla T4 with `torch=2.10.0+cu128`, `backend=fast`; best direct forward was `batch=2048`, `734786.8` candidates/s, and searcher-like `batch_process` for `65536` rows with `eval_batch_size=16384` was `630697.0` candidates/s. Evidence is recorded in `test_results/transformer_inference_example_kaggle_speed_2026-07-01.md`.

## 2026-07-03

- Ran Kaggle 2xT4 benchmark version 11 against tag `stream1-transformer-fmha-44352f1`. The CUTLASS FMHA attention route completed successfully with best T4 throughput `502218.5` candidates/s on GPU0 and `500790.0` on GPU1, aggregate `1003008.5` candidates/s. - Improved the Stream1 `piece_transformer` FMHA route by removing the explicit QKV repack kernel and passing the original QKV projection buffer directly to CUTLASS FMHA via strided Q/K/V pointers. # Stream1 Piece Transformer Kaggle 2xT4 v12 Strided FMHA Benchmark

## Scope

Validate the strided-QKV CUTLASS FMHA route on Kaggle 2xT4.

- Kernel: `trydotatwo/cayley-beam-transformer-2xt4-benchmark`
- Kaggle version: `12`
- Source ref: `stream1-transformer-strided-fmha-6d29ac4`
- Expected commit prefix: `6d29ac4`
- Runtime mode: `BEAM_STREAM1_TRANSFORMER_GRAPH_BENCH=1`
- Status: `KernelWorkerStatus.COMPLETE`

## Output Location

Downloaded Kaggle artifacts:

- `test_results/kaggle_stream1_transformer_2xt4_v12_strided_fmha_2026-07-03/`
- Main log: `test_results/kaggle_stream1_transformer_2xt4_v12_strided_fmha_2026-07-03/cayley-beam-transformer-2xt4-benchmark.log`
- CSV: `test_results/kaggle_stream1_transformer_2xt4_v12_strided_fmha_2026-07-03/stream1_transformer_benchmark_rows.csv`
- Per-GPU reports: `test_results/kaggle_stream1_transformer_2xt4_v12_strided_fmha_2026-07-03/stream1_transformer_benchmark_reports/`

## Results

Best rows:

- GPU0: `b_micro=512`, `concurrency=2`, `candidates_per_sec=573280.3`, `scratch_bytes=327729152`
- GPU1: `b_micro=512`, `concurrency=2`, `candidates_per_sec=560959.8`, `scratch_bytes=327729152`
- Aggregate: `STREAM1_TRANSFORMER_BEST_2XT4_AGG_CANDIDATES_PER_SEC=1134240.1`

## Comparison

Kaggle v11 packed-QKV FMHA:

- GPU0: `502218.5` candidates/s
- GPU1: `500790.0` candidates/s
- Aggregate: `1003008.5` candidates/s

Strided-QKV v12 is therefore about:

- GPU0: `1.142x` of v11
- GPU1: `1.120x` of v11
- Aggregate: `1.131x` of v11

Previous v10 graph replay before FMHA:

- Aggregate: `930978.0` candidates/s

Strided-QKV v12 is `1.218x` of v10 aggregate.

PyTorch reference from the transformer inference example was about `630697.0` candidates/s per T4 in searcher-like `batch_process` mode. v12 reaches roughly:

- GPU0: `0.909x` of PyTorch
- GPU1: `0.889x` of PyTorch
- Aggregate vs two T4 reference: `0.899x`

## Interpretation

Removing the explicit QKV repack closes most of the previous native-vs-PyTorch SDPA gap. The remaining gap is no longer the old decomposed attention chain; it is likely in the remaining transformer kernels and CUTLASS FMHA/kernel choices versus PyTorch's tuned SDPA path.

# Stream1 Piece Transformer Kaggle 2xT4 v12 Strided FMHA Benchmark

## Scope

Validate the strided-QKV CUTLASS FMHA route on Kaggle 2xT4.

- Kernel: `trydotatwo/cayley-beam-transformer-2xt4-benchmark`
- Kaggle version: `12`
- Source ref: `stream1-transformer-strided-fmha-6d29ac4`
- Expected commit prefix: `6d29ac4`
- Runtime mode: `BEAM_STREAM1_TRANSFORMER_GRAPH_BENCH=1`
- Status: `KernelWorkerStatus.COMPLETE`

## Output Location

Downloaded Kaggle artifacts:

- `test_results/kaggle_stream1_transformer_2xt4_v12_strided_fmha_2026-07-03/`
- Main log: `test_results/kaggle_stream1_transformer_2xt4_v12_strided_fmha_2026-07-03/cayley-beam-transformer-2xt4-benchmark.log`
- CSV: `test_results/kaggle_stream1_transformer_2xt4_v12_strided_fmha_2026-07-03/stream1_transformer_benchmark_rows.csv`
- Per-GPU reports: `test_results/kaggle_stream1_transformer_2xt4_v12_strided_fmha_2026-07-03/stream1_transformer_benchmark_reports/`

## Results

Best rows:

- GPU0: `b_micro=512`, `concurrency=2`, `candidates_per_sec=573280.3`, `scratch_bytes=327729152`
- GPU1: `b_micro=512`, `concurrency=2`, `candidates_per_sec=560959.8`, `scratch_bytes=327729152`
- Aggregate: `STREAM1_TRANSFORMER_BEST_2XT4_AGG_CANDIDATES_PER_SEC=1134240.1`

## Comparison

Kaggle v11 packed-QKV FMHA:

- GPU0: `502218.5` candidates/s
- GPU1: `500790.0` candidates/s
- Aggregate: `1003008.5` candidates/s

Strided-QKV v12 is therefore about:

- GPU0: `1.142x` of v11
- GPU1: `1.120x` of v11
- Aggregate: `1.131x` of v11

Previous v10 graph replay before FMHA:

- Aggregate: `930978.0` candidates/s

Strided-QKV v12 is `1.218x` of v10 aggregate.

PyTorch reference from the transformer inference example was about `630697.0` candidates/s per T4 in searcher-like `batch_process` mode. v12 reaches roughly:

- GPU0: `0.909x` of PyTorch
- GPU1: `0.889x` of PyTorch
- Aggregate vs two T4 reference: `0.899x`

## Interpretation

Removing the explicit QKV repack closes most of the previous native-vs-PyTorch SDPA gap. The remaining gap is no longer the old decomposed attention chain; it is likely in the remaining transformer kernels and CUTLASS FMHA/kernel choices versus PyTorch's tuned SDPA path.

# HighloadGpu

Router for CUDA code-writing and high-performance GPU engineering. Default to a single-GPU CUDA hot path first; use multi-GPU or search/decoding guidance only when the task calls for it.

## Pick The Sub-Skill

- CUDA kernels, memory layout, CUTLASS/CUB, graphs, native hot paths: `write-cuda-hot-paths`
- Beam search, top-k/top-p decoding, frontier expansion, candidate selection: `optimize-gpu-search-and-decoding`
- Multi-GPU scaling, rank ownership, peer access, NCCL, overlap: `design-multigpu-systems`
- Python/Rust/C++/CUDA ownership boundaries: `choose-stack-boundaries`
- GPU model, compute capability, CUDA/library docs: `use-nvidia-docs`
- Timeline/stream/NCCL/launch gaps: `use-nsight-systems`
- One-kernel bottleneck: `use-nsight-compute`
- Illegal access/race/init/sync bug: `use-compute-sanitizer`
- Batch/concurrency/shard sweeps: `benchmark-and-sweep-gpu-configs`
- Kaggle/Molab/remote GPU profiling: `profile-remote-gpu-runs`

## Defaults

- Python: wrappers, notebooks, dashboards, CLI/torchrun launch.
- Rust: safe config, validation, artifact/log tooling, host services.
- C++ + CUDA: CPU/GPU hot paths, kernels, CUDA Graphs, NCCL, CUTLASS, CUB/CCCL.

Check current NVIDIA docs before hardware-specific advice. Require correctness checks and profiling evidence before architecture changes.

---
name: write-cuda-hot-paths
description: Use when writing or optimizing CUDA kernels, memory layouts, and GPU hot paths.
---

# Write CUDA Hot Paths

Primary skill for CUDA code-writing. Hot paths are fixed-capacity, allocation-free, profiler-driven, and explicit about layout, alignment, ownership, and synchronization.

## Workflow

1. State shapes, precision, target GPU, correctness oracle, and measured bottleneck.
2. Choose library vs custom kernel; use custom CUDA where layout, fusion, or control flow makes it worthwhile.
3. Design layout first, implement a small deterministic path, then profile.

## Rules

- Allocate device memory, library temp, NCCL buffers, and graph resources before repeated loops.
- Use explicit capacity guards; fail loudly on overflow.
- Keep CPU readback out of the steady-state path.
- Use CUDA Graphs for repeated launch templates; keep dynamic dispatch on host.
- Add static asserts for cross-kernel metadata size/alignment.
- Store only downstream-needed data; avoid materializing large intermediates when compact keys, indices, or reductions are enough.

## Library Defaults

CUTLASS/cuBLAS for GEMM/tensor-core kernels; CUB/CCCL for sort/reduce/scan/select; NCCL for GPU exchange/collectives; CUDA Runtime/Driver APIs for memory, streams, events, graphs, devices, and peer access.

## Avoid

Dynamic `cudaMalloc`, Python data-plane loops, fine-grained atomics when partition/sort/scan works, custom sort before checking CUB/CCCL, and synchronization that hides ownership bugs.

# Project Agent Rules

## Operating Rule
- Read `AGENTS.md` before project edits.
- Update `memory/CHANGELOG.md` after meaningful code, config, or architecture changes.
- Update `memory/PROMPTS.md` with user prompts that define requirements.
- Store test outputs, logs, and verification notes under `test_results/`.
- Prefer agent-centered code: explicit contracts, deterministic tests, small files, low hidden state.

## Architecture Source
- Primary architecture contract: `ARCHITECTURE_NEED.md`.
- Current Stream 4 implementation rule: use threshold + compact + CUB/fixed-temp sort/reduce + compact; do not use Stream 4 hash-table dedup.

## Implementation Guardrails
- `State128` logical bytes are `v[0..119]`.
- `State128` padding bytes are `v[120..127]`.
- Persistent frontier padding must be zero.
- `FinalResponse` may temporarily store `target_local_idx` in `v[120..123]`.
- `Hash128` is one logical 128-bit key stored as `{lo, hi}`.
- `CandidateMeta` must remain 32 bytes and 32-byte aligned.
- Stream 3 payload id must be original candidate id, not compact index.
- Stream 4 must not apply shard top-k or semantic shard cap.

# HighloadGpu

Router for CUDA code-writing and high-performance GPU engineering. Default to a single-GPU CUDA hot path first; use multi-GPU or search/decoding guidance only when the task calls for it.

## Pick The Sub-Skill

- CUDA kernels, memory layout, CUTLASS/CUB, graphs, native hot paths: `write-cuda-hot-paths`
- Beam search, top-k/top-p decoding, frontier expansion, candidate selection: `optimize-gpu-search-and-decoding`
- Multi-GPU scaling, rank ownership, peer access, NCCL, overlap: `design-multigpu-systems`
- Python/Rust/C++/CUDA ownership boundaries: `choose-stack-boundaries`
- GPU model, compute capability, CUDA/library docs: `use-nvidia-docs`
- Timeline/stream/NCCL/launch gaps: `use-nsight-systems`
- One-kernel bottleneck: `use-nsight-compute`
- Illegal access/race/init/sync bug: `use-compute-sanitizer`
- Batch/concurrency/shard sweeps: `benchmark-and-sweep-gpu-configs`
- Kaggle/Molab/remote GPU profiling: `profile-remote-gpu-runs`

## Defaults

- Python: wrappers, notebooks, dashboards, CLI/torchrun launch.
- Rust: safe config, validation, artifact/log tooling, host services.
- C++ + CUDA: CPU/GPU hot paths, kernels, CUDA Graphs, NCCL, CUTLASS, CUB/CCCL.

Check current NVIDIA docs before hardware-specific advice. Require correctness checks and profiling evidence before architecture changes.

---
name: write-cuda-hot-paths
description: Use when writing or optimizing CUDA kernels, memory layouts, and GPU hot paths.
---

# Write CUDA Hot Paths

Primary skill for CUDA code-writing. Hot paths are fixed-capacity, allocation-free, profiler-driven, and explicit about layout, alignment, ownership, and synchronization.

## Workflow

1. State shapes, precision, target GPU, correctness oracle, and measured bottleneck.
2. Choose library vs custom kernel; use custom CUDA where layout, fusion, or control flow makes it worthwhile.
3. Design layout first, implement a small deterministic path, then profile.

## Rules

- Allocate device memory, library temp, NCCL buffers, and graph resources before repeated loops.
- Use explicit capacity guards; fail loudly on overflow.
- Keep CPU readback out of the steady-state path.
- Use CUDA Graphs for repeated launch templates; keep dynamic dispatch on host.
- Add static asserts for cross-kernel metadata size/alignment.
- Store only downstream-needed data; avoid materializing large intermediates when compact keys, indices, or reductions are enough.

## Library Defaults

CUTLASS/cuBLAS for GEMM/tensor-core kernels; CUB/CCCL for sort/reduce/scan/select; NCCL for GPU exchange/collectives; CUDA Runtime/Driver APIs for memory, streams, events, graphs, devices, and peer access.

## Avoid

Dynamic `cudaMalloc`, Python data-plane loops, fine-grained atomics when partition/sort/scan works, custom sort before checking CUB/CCCL, and synchronization that hides ownership bugs.

# Project Agent Rules

## Operating Rule
- Read `AGENTS.md` before project edits.
- Update `memory/CHANGELOG.md` after meaningful code, config, or architecture changes.
- Update `memory/PROMPTS.md` with user prompts that define requirements.
- Store test outputs, logs, and verification notes under `test_results/`.
- Prefer agent-centered code: explicit contracts, deterministic tests, small files, low hidden state.

## Architecture Source
- Primary architecture contract: `ARCHITECTURE_NEED.md`.
- Current Stream 4 implementation rule: use threshold + compact + CUB/fixed-temp sort/reduce + compact; do not use Stream 4 hash-table dedup.

## Implementation Guardrails
- `State128` logical bytes are `v[0..119]`.
- `State128` padding bytes are `v[120..127]`.
- Persistent frontier padding must be zero.
- `FinalResponse` may temporarily store `target_local_idx` in `v[120..123]`.
- `Hash128` is one logical 128-bit key stored as `{lo, hi}`.
- `CandidateMeta` must remain 32 bytes and 32-byte aligned.
- Stream 3 payload id must be original candidate id, not compact index.
- Stream 4 must not apply shard top-k or semantic shard cap.

# Use Nsight Systems

Use Nsight Systems for stream idle gaps, CPU launch/sync blocks, and NCCL/compute overlap.

```bash
nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt,cublas,nccl --stats=true --force-overwrite=true -o nsys_run ./runner ...
nsys stats nsys_run.nsys-rep
nsys export --type sqlite --force-overwrite=true -o nsys_run.sqlite nsys_run.nsys-rep
```

Profile a bounded window. Add NVTX around batch, stage, stream, rank, shard, communication, and pipeline phase.

Inspect stream overlap, idle gaps, long CUDA API calls, graph replay/instantiation, NCCL order, host blocking, and log alignment.

# Use Nsight Compute

Use Nsight Compute after evidence points to one kernel.

```bash
ncu --set full --target-processes all --kernel-name regex:kernel_name --launch-skip 5 --launch-count 10 --force-overwrite -o ncu_kernel ./runner ...

Do not use NCU first for whole-pipeline scheduling; use Nsight Systems.

## Current committed code

- Code commit under test: `e35432dc475e3eb5b900b0470fe57f72e07f3d18` (`stream1-transformer-graph-bench-e35432d`).

```bash

./build-stream1-opt/stream_benchmark 991
```

Result before profiling overhead:

```text
stream1_transformer_micro b_micro=1024 concurrency=2 rows_per_launch_group=2048 ms_per_launch_group=84.3790 parents_per_sec=24271.5 candidates_per_sec=582514.8 scratch_bytes=655458304
```

## Nsight Systems graph-node profile

Profile command used `--cuda-graph-trace=node` so CUDA graph node kernels are included in `cuda_gpu_kern_sum`.

Top GPU kernel buckets at `1024x2` under profiler overhead:

```text
22.7%  CUTLASS GEMM group, 126 launches
20.4%  CUTLASS fused-epilogue GEMM group, 56 launches
14.9%  stream1_transformer_layernorm256_copy_kernel, 126 launches
13.7%  CUTLASS fused-epilogue GEMM group, 56 launches
 7.8%  CUTLASS GemmBatched group, 448 launches
 5.3%  stream1_transformer_bias_add_kernel, 112 launches

 1.3%  stream1_transformer_build_input_kernel, 14 launches
```

Interpretation:

- Remaining gap is mostly transformer linear GEMMs plus LayerNorm/copy and attention layout kernels.
- Build-input and score quantization are not the next bottleneck.
- Launch overhead is no longer the dominant explanation once graph replay is used.

## Rejected experiment: cuBLASLt QKV

A temporary experiment replaced only the QKV linear+bias with cuBLASLt and kept graph replay timing.

Verification:

stream1_transformer_cuda_tests=pass

```

Decision:

- Reject cuBLASLt QKV for now. It is slower than the committed CUTLASS QKV graph replay path (`354878.7` vs `582514.8` candidates/s locally).
- The experimental source files and CMake changes were removed; no cuBLASLt runtime path is committed.

## Operating Rule
- Read `AGENTS.md` before project edits.
- Update `memory/CHANGELOG.md` after meaningful code, config, or architecture changes.
- Update `memory/PROMPTS.md` with user prompts that define requirements.
- Store test outputs, logs, and verification notes under `test_results/`.

- `State128` logical bytes are `v[0..119]`.

- `CandidateMeta` must remain 32 bytes and 32-byte aligned.
- Stream 3 payload id must be original candidate id, not compact index.
- Stream 4 must not apply shard top-k or semantic shard cap.

# HighloadGpu

Router for CUDA code-writing and high-performance GPU engineering. Default to a single-GPU CUDA hot path first; use multi-GPU or search/decoding guidance only when the task calls for it.

## Pick The Sub-Skill

- CUDA kernels, memory layout, CUTLASS/CUB, graphs, native hot paths: `write-cuda-hot-paths`
- Beam search, top-k/top-p decoding, frontier expansion, candidate selection: `optimize-gpu-search-and-decoding`
- Multi-GPU scaling, rank ownership, peer access, NCCL, overlap: `design-multigpu-systems`
- Python/Rust/C++/CUDA ownership boundaries: `choose-stack-boundaries`
- GPU model, compute capability, CUDA/library docs: `use-nvidia-docs`
- Timeline/stream/NCCL/launch gaps: `use-nsight-systems`
- One-kernel bottleneck: `use-nsight-compute`
- Illegal access/race/init/sync bug: `use-compute-sanitizer`
- Batch/concurrency/shard sweeps: `benchmark-and-sweep-gpu-configs`
- Kaggle/Molab/remote GPU profiling: `profile-remote-gpu-runs`

## Defaults

- Python: wrappers, notebooks, dashboards, CLI/torchrun launch.
- Rust: safe config, validation, artifact/log tooling, host services.
- C++ + CUDA: CPU/GPU hot paths, kernels, CUDA Graphs, NCCL, CUTLASS, CUB/CCCL.

Check current NVIDIA docs before hardware-specific advice. Require correctness checks and profiling evidence before architecture changes.

name: write-cuda-hot-paths
description: Use when writing or optimizing CUDA kernels, memory layouts, and GPU hot paths.
---

# Write CUDA Hot Paths

Primary skill for CUDA code-writing. Hot paths are fixed-capacity, allocation-free, profiler-driven, and explicit about layout, alignment, ownership, and synchronization.

## Workflow

1. State shapes, precision, target GPU, correctness oracle, and measured bottleneck.
2. Choose library vs custom kernel; use custom CUDA where layout, fusion, or control flow makes it worthwhile.
3. Design layout first, implement a small deterministic path, then profile.

## Rules

- Allocate device memory, library temp, NCCL buffers, and graph resources before repeated loops.
- Use explicit capacity guards; fail loudly on overflow.
- Keep CPU readback out of the steady-state path.
- Use CUDA Graphs for repeated launch templates; keep dynamic dispatch on host.
- Add static asserts for cross-kernel metadata size/alignment.
- Store only downstream-needed data; avoid materializing large intermediates when compact keys, indices, or reductions are enough.

## Library Defaults

CUTLASS/cuBLAS for GEMM/tensor-core kernels; CUB/CCCL for sort/reduce/scan/select; NCCL for GPU exchange/collectives; CUDA Runtime/Driver APIs for memory, streams, events, graphs, devices, and peer access.

## Avoid

Dynamic `cudaMalloc`, Python data-plane loops, fine-grained atomics when partition/sort/scan works, custom sort before checking CUB/CCCL, and synchronization that hides ownership bugs.

# Use Nsight Systems

Use Nsight Systems for stream idle gaps, CPU launch/sync blocks, and NCCL/compute overlap.

```bash

# Project Agent Rules

## Operating Rule
- Read `AGENTS.md` before project edits.
- Update `memory/CHANGELOG.md` after meaningful code, config, or architecture changes.
- Update `memory/PROMPTS.md` with user prompts that define requirements.
- Store test outputs, logs, and verification notes under `test_results/`.
- Prefer agent-centered code: explicit contracts, deterministic tests, small files, low hidden state.

## Architecture Source
- Primary architecture contract: `ARCHITECTURE_NEED.md`.
- Current Stream 4 implementation rule: use threshold + compact + CUB/fixed-temp sort/reduce + compact; do not use Stream 4 hash-table dedup.

## Implementation Guardrails
- `State128` logical bytes are `v[0..119]`.
- `State128` padding bytes are `v[120..127]`.
- Persistent frontier padding must be zero.
- `FinalResponse` may temporarily store `target_local_idx` in `v[120..123]`.
- `Hash128` is one logical 128-bit key stored as `{lo, hi}`.
- `CandidateMeta` must remain 32 bytes and 32-byte aligned.
- Stream 3 payload id must be original candidate id, not compact index.
- Stream 4 must not apply shard top-k or semantic shard cap.

# HighloadGpu

Router for CUDA code-writing and high-performance GPU engineering. Default to a single-GPU CUDA hot path first; use multi-GPU or search/decoding guidance only when the task calls for it.

## Pick The Sub-Skill

- CUDA kernels, memory layout, CUTLASS/CUB, graphs, native hot paths: `write-cuda-hot-paths`
- Beam search, top-k/top-p decoding, frontier expansion, candidate selection: `optimize-gpu-search-and-decoding`
- Multi-GPU scaling, rank ownership, peer access, NCCL, overlap: `design-multigpu-systems`
- Python/Rust/C++/CUDA ownership boundaries: `choose-stack-boundaries`
- GPU model, compute capability, CUDA/library docs: `use-nvidia-docs`
- Timeline/stream/NCCL/launch gaps: `use-nsight-systems`
- One-kernel bottleneck: `use-nsight-compute`
- Illegal access/race/init/sync bug: `use-compute-sanitizer`
- Batch/concurrency/shard sweeps: `benchmark-and-sweep-gpu-configs`
- Kaggle/Molab/remote GPU profiling: `profile-remote-gpu-runs`

## Defaults

- Python: wrappers, notebooks, dashboards, CLI/torchrun launch.
- Rust: safe config, validation, artifact/log tooling, host services.
- C++ + CUDA: CPU/GPU hot paths, kernels, CUDA Graphs, NCCL, CUTLASS, CUB/CCCL.

Check current NVIDIA docs before hardware-specific advice. Require correctness checks and profiling evidence before architecture changes.

---
name: write-cuda-hot-paths
description: Use when writing or optimizing CUDA kernels, memory layouts, and GPU hot paths.
---

# Write CUDA Hot Paths

Primary skill for CUDA code-writing. Hot paths are fixed-capacity, allocation-free, profiler-driven, and explicit about layout, alignment, ownership, and synchronization.

## Workflow

1. State shapes, precision, target GPU, correctness oracle, and measured bottleneck.
2. Choose library vs custom kernel; use custom CUDA where layout, fusion, or control flow makes it worthwhile.
3. Design layout first, implement a small deterministic path, then profile.

## Rules

- Allocate device memory, library temp, NCCL buffers, and graph resources before repeated loops.
- Use explicit capacity guards; fail loudly on overflow.
- Keep CPU readback out of the steady-state path.
- Use CUDA Graphs for repeated launch templates; keep dynamic dispatch on host.
- Add static asserts for cross-kernel metadata size/alignment.
- Store only downstream-needed data; avoid materializing large intermediates when compact keys, indices, or reductions are enough.

## Library Defaults

CUTLASS/cuBLAS for GEMM/tensor-core kernels; CUB/CCCL for sort/reduce/scan/select; NCCL for GPU exchange/collectives; CUDA Runtime/Driver APIs for memory, streams, events, graphs, devices, and peer access.

## Avoid

Dynamic `cudaMalloc`, Python data-plane loops, fine-grained atomics when partition/sort/scan works, custom sort before checking CUB/CCCL, and synchronization that hides ownership bugs.

name: use-nsight-systems
description: Use when analyzing GPU timelines.

# Use Nsight Systems

Use Nsight Systems for stream idle gaps, CPU launch/sync blocks, and NCCL/compute overlap.

```bash
nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt,cublas,nccl --stats=true --force-overwrite=true -o nsys_run ./runner ...
nsys stats nsys_run.nsys-rep
nsys export --type sqlite --force-overwrite=true -o nsys_run.sqlite nsys_run.nsys-rep
```

Profile a bounded window. Add NVTX around batch, stage, stream, rank, shard, communication, and pipeline phase.

Inspect stream overlap, idle gaps, long CUDA API calls, graph replay/instantiation, NCCL order, host blocking, and log alignment.

# Use Nsight Compute

Use Nsight Compute after evidence points to one kernel.

```bash
ncu --set full --target-processes all --kernel-name regex:kernel_name --launch-skip 5 --launch-count 10 --force-overwrite -o ncu_kernel ./runner ...
```

Prefer small reproductions. Check critical-path kernel, occupancy limiter, memory throughput/load efficiency, stalls, tensor-core use, and register/shared-memory pressure.

Do not use NCU first for whole-pipeline scheduling; use Nsight Systems.

# Stream1 Piece Transformer Kaggle 2xT4 v12 Strided FMHA Benchmark

## Scope

Validate the strided-QKV CUTLASS FMHA route on Kaggle 2xT4.

- Kernel: `trydotatwo/cayley-beam-transformer-2xt4-benchmark`
- Kaggle version: `12`
- Source ref: `stream1-transformer-strided-fmha-6d29ac4`
- Expected commit prefix: `6d29ac4`
- Runtime mode: `BEAM_STREAM1_TRANSFORMER_GRAPH_BENCH=1`
- Status: `KernelWorkerStatus.COMPLETE`

## Output Location

Downloaded Kaggle artifacts:

- `test_results/kaggle_stream1_transformer_2xt4_v12_strided_fmha_2026-07-03/`
- Main log: `test_results/kaggle_stream1_transformer_2xt4_v12_strided_fmha_2026-07-03/cayley-beam-transformer-2xt4-benchmark.log`
- CSV: `test_results/kaggle_stream1_transformer_2xt4_v12_strided_fmha_2026-07-03/stream1_transformer_benchmark_rows.csv`
- Per-GPU reports: `test_results/kaggle_stream1_transformer_2xt4_v12_strided_fmha_2026-07-03/stream1_transformer_benchmark_reports/`

## Results

Best rows:

- GPU0: `b_micro=512`, `concurrency=2`, `candidates_per_sec=573280.3`, `scratch_bytes=327729152`
- GPU1: `b_micro=512`, `concurrency=2`, `candidates_per_sec=560959.8`, `scratch_bytes=327729152`
- Aggregate: `STREAM1_TRANSFORMER_BEST_2XT4_AGG_CANDIDATES_PER_SEC=1134240.1`

## Comparison

Kaggle v11 packed-QKV FMHA:

- GPU0: `502218.5` candidates/s
- GPU1: `500790.0` candidates/s
- Aggregate: `1003008.5` candidates/s

Strided-QKV v12 is therefore about:

- GPU0: `1.142x` of v11
- GPU1: `1.120x` of v11
- Aggregate: `1.131x` of v11

Previous v10 graph replay before FMHA:

- Aggregate: `930978.0` candidates/s

Strided-QKV v12 is `1.218x` of v10 aggregate.

PyTorch reference from the transformer inference example was about `630697.0` candidates/s per T4 in searcher-like `batch_process` mode. v12 reaches roughly:

- GPU0: `0.909x` of PyTorch
- GPU1: `0.889x` of PyTorch
- Aggregate vs two T4 reference: `0.899x`

## Interpretation

Removing the explicit QKV repack closes most of the previous native-vs-PyTorch SDPA gap. The remaining gap is no longer the old decomposed attention chain; it is likely in the remaining transformer kernels and CUTLASS FMHA/kernel choices versus PyTorch's tuned SDPA path.

## Current committed code

- Code commit under test: `e35432dc475e3eb5b900b0470fe57f72e07f3d18` (`stream1-transformer-graph-bench-e35432d`).

## Local graph replay benchmark

```bash

Result before profiling overhead:

```text

```

## Nsight Systems graph-node profile

Profile command used `--cuda-graph-trace=node` so CUDA graph node kernels are included in `cuda_gpu_kern_sum`.

Top GPU kernel buckets at `1024x2` under profiler overhead:

```text
22.7%  CUTLASS GEMM group, 126 launches
20.4%  CUTLASS fused-epilogue GEMM group, 56 launches
14.9%  stream1_transformer_layernorm256_copy_kernel, 126 launches
13.7%  CUTLASS fused-epilogue GEMM group, 56 launches

 5.3%  stream1_transformer_bias_add_kernel, 112 launches
 5.3%  stream1_transformer_softmax51_kernel, 56 launches
 4.7%  stream1_transformer_pack_v51_kernel, 56 launches
 3.8%  CUTLASS GemmBatched group, 448 launches
 1.3%  stream1_transformer_build_input_kernel, 14 launches
```

Interpretation:

- Remaining gap is mostly transformer linear GEMMs plus LayerNorm/copy and attention layout kernels.
- Build-input and score quantization are not the next bottleneck.
- Launch overhead is no longer the dominant explanation once graph replay is used.

## Rejected experiment: cuBLASLt QKV

A temporary experiment replaced only the QKV linear+bias with cuBLASLt and kept graph replay timing.

Verification:

```text
stream1_transformer_cuda_tests=pass
dispatcher_cuda_tests=pass

```

Decision:

- Reject cuBLASLt QKV for now. It is slower than the committed CUTLASS QKV graph replay path (`354878.7` vs `582514.8` candidates/s locally).
- The experimental source files and CMake changes were removed; no cuBLASLt runtime path is committed.

# Stream1 Piece Transformer Kaggle 2xT4 v12 Strided FMHA Benchmark

## Scope

Validate the strided-QKV CUTLASS FMHA route on Kaggle 2xT4.

- Kernel: `trydotatwo/cayley-beam-transformer-2xt4-benchmark`
- Kaggle version: `12`
- Source ref: `stream1-transformer-strided-fmha-6d29ac4`
- Expected commit prefix: `6d29ac4`
- Runtime mode: `BEAM_STREAM1_TRANSFORMER_GRAPH_BENCH=1`
- Status: `KernelWorkerStatus.COMPLETE`

## Output Location

Downloaded Kaggle artifacts:

- `test_results/kaggle_stream1_transformer_2xt4_v12_strided_fmha_2026-07-03/`
- Main log: `test_results/kaggle_stream1_transformer_2xt4_v12_strided_fmha_2026-07-03/cayley-beam-transformer-2xt4-benchmark.log`
- CSV: `test_results/kaggle_stream1_transformer_2xt4_v12_strided_fmha_2026-07-03/stream1_transformer_benchmark_rows.csv`
- Per-GPU reports: `test_results/kaggle_stream1_transformer_2xt4_v12_strided_fmha_2026-07-03/stream1_transformer_benchmark_reports/`

## Results

Best rows:

- GPU0: `b_micro=512`, `concurrency=2`, `candidates_per_sec=573280.3`, `scratch_bytes=327729152`
- GPU1: `b_micro=512`, `concurrency=2`, `candidates_per_sec=560959.8`, `scratch_bytes=327729152`
- Aggregate: `STREAM1_TRANSFORMER_BEST_2XT4_AGG_CANDIDATES_PER_SEC=1134240.1`

## Comparison

Kaggle v11 packed-QKV FMHA:

- GPU0: `502218.5` candidates/s
- GPU1: `500790.0` candidates/s
- Aggregate: `1003008.5` candidates/s

Strided-QKV v12 is therefore about:

- GPU0: `1.142x` of v11
- GPU1: `1.120x` of v11
- Aggregate: `1.131x` of v11

Previous v10 graph replay before FMHA:

- Aggregate: `930978.0` candidates/s

Strided-QKV v12 is `1.218x` of v10 aggregate.

PyTorch reference from the transformer inference example was about `630697.0` candidates/s per T4 in searcher-like `batch_process` mode. v12 reaches roughly:

- GPU0: `0.909x` of PyTorch
- GPU1: `0.889x` of PyTorch
- Aggregate vs two T4 reference: `0.899x`

## Interpretation

Removing the explicit QKV repack closes most of the previous native-vs-PyTorch SDPA gap. The remaining gap is no longer the old decomposed attention chain; it is likely in the remaining transformer kernels and CUTLASS FMHA/kernel choices versus PyTorch's tuned SDPA path.

# Stream1 Transformer Graph Profile 2026-07-03

## Current committed code

- Code commit under test: `e35432dc475e3eb5b900b0470fe57f72e07f3d18` (`stream1-transformer-graph-bench-e35432d`).
- Kaggle package commit: `32562e4`, notebook pins the code checkout to that tag and sets `BEAM_STREAM1_TRANSFORMER_GRAPH_BENCH=1`.
- Kaggle push was attempted twice after the package update and failed with `Maximum batch GPU session count of 2 reached`.
- Visible running Kaggle kernel found: `trydotatwo/rogii-tabfm-zero-shot-context-ensemble`.

## Local graph replay benchmark

Command shape:

```bash
BEAM_WEIGHT_DIR=test_results/kaggle_stream1_transformer_2xt4_v9_qkv_fused_2026-07-03/stream1_transformer_weights_fp16 \
BEAM_STREAM1_TRANSFORMER_GRAPH_BENCH=1 \
BEAM_STREAM1_TRANSFORMER_B_MICRO=1024 \
BEAM_STREAM1_TRANSFORMER_CONCURRENCY=2 \
./build-stream1-opt/stream_benchmark 991
```

Result before profiling overhead:

```text
stream1_transformer_micro b_micro=1024 concurrency=2 rows_per_launch_group=2048 ms_per_launch_group=84.3790 parents_per_sec=24271.5 candidates_per_sec=582514.8 scratch_bytes=655458304
```

## Nsight Systems graph-node profile

Profile command used `--cuda-graph-trace=node` so CUDA graph node kernels are included in `cuda_gpu_kern_sum`.

Top GPU kernel buckets at `1024x2` under profiler overhead:

```text
22.7%  CUTLASS GEMM group, 126 launches
20.4%  CUTLASS fused-epilogue GEMM group, 56 launches
14.9%  stream1_transformer_layernorm256_copy_kernel, 126 launches
13.7%  CUTLASS fused-epilogue GEMM group, 56 launches
 7.8%  CUTLASS GemmBatched group, 448 launches
 5.3%  stream1_transformer_bias_add_kernel, 112 launches
 5.3%  stream1_transformer_softmax51_kernel, 56 launches
 4.7%  stream1_transformer_pack_v51_kernel, 56 launches
 3.8%  CUTLASS GemmBatched group, 448 launches
 1.3%  stream1_transformer_build_input_kernel, 14 launches
```

Interpretation:

- Remaining gap is mostly transformer linear GEMMs plus LayerNorm/copy and attention layout kernels.
- Build-input and score quantization are not the next bottleneck.
- Launch overhead is no longer the dominant explanation once graph replay is used.

## Rejected experiment: cuBLASLt QKV

A temporary experiment replaced only the QKV linear+bias with cuBLASLt and kept graph replay timing.

Verification:

```text
stream1_transformer_cuda_tests=pass
dispatcher_cuda_tests=pass
stream1_transformer_micro b_micro=1024 concurrency=2 rows_per_launch_group=2048 ms_per_launch_group=138.5037 parents_per_sec=14786.6 candidates_per_sec=354878.7 scratch_bytes=655458304
```

Decision:

- Reject cuBLASLt QKV for now. It is slower than the committed CUTLASS QKV graph replay path (`354878.7` vs `582514.8` candidates/s locally).
- The experimental source files and CMake changes were removed; no cuBLASLt runtime path is committed.

void stream1_transformer_linear_residual_cuda(
    const half* input,
    const half* weight,
    half* residual_inout,
    std::uint32_t rows,
    std::uint32_t input_cols,
    std::uint32_t output_cols,
    std::uint32_t dtype,
    cudaStream_t stream) {
    if (dtype == STREAM1_DTYPE_BF16) {
        int device = 0;
        cudaDeviceProp prop{};
        BEAM_CUDA_CHECK(cudaGetDevice(&device));
        BEAM_CUDA_CHECK(cudaGetDeviceProperties(&prop, device));
        if (prop.major < 8) {
            throw std::invalid_argument("Stream1 piece_transformer bf16 residual GEMM requires SM80+");
        }
        stream1_transformer_linear_residual_typed<
            cutlass::bfloat16_t,
            cutlass::arch::Sm80,
            cutlass::gemm::GemmShape<16, 8, 16>>(input, weight, residual_inout, rows, input_cols, output_cols, stream);

    if (dtype == STREAM1_DTYPE_FP16) {
        stream1_transformer_linear_residual_typed<

        return;
    }
    throw std::invalid_argument("Stream1 piece_transformer residual GEMM dtype must be fp16 or bf16");
}
